questions.question: Describe the Earth's revolution, including its period, the angle and direction of the axis, and the change in distance from the sun. Explain why the distance is not the cause of the seasons.
questions.expected_answer: The Earth revolves around the sun in about 365¼ days, with an extra day every fourth year in a leap year. Its orbit is nearly circular, at an average of about 150 million km. The axis is tilted about 23,5° from the vertical and always points in the same direction in space, so each hemisphere leans towards the sun for half the year and away for the other half. The Earth is closest to the sun, about 147 million km, in early January and furthest, about 152 million km, in early July. Distance is not the cause of the seasons because the Earth is closest in January, which is winter in the Northern Hemisphere, and the difference is only about three percent.

questions.question: Name and date the two solstices and two equinoxes, state where the midday sun is overhead on each, and explain what happens to day length in South Africa on each date.
questions.expected_answer: December solstice, about 21 or 22 December: sun overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, 23,5°S; South Africa's summer solstice and longest day. June solstice, about 21 June: sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, 23,5°N; South Africa's winter solstice and shortest day. Autumn equinox in South Africa, about 21 March, and spring equinox, about 23 September: sun overhead at the equator; day and night about twelve hours each.

questions.question: Calculate the angle of the midday sun in Johannesburg, at 26°S, on 21 December and on 21 June, showing your working, and explain why the difference affects temperature.
questions.expected_answer: 21 December: sun overhead at 23,5°S, same hemisphere, so 26 − 23,5 = 2,5, and the angle is 90 − 2,5 = 87,5°. 21 June: sun overhead at 23,5°N, opposite hemisphere, so 26 + 23,5 = 49,5, and the angle is 90 − 49,5 = 40,5°. A high sun concentrates its energy on a smaller area and passes through less atmosphere, heating the ground strongly; a low sun spreads the same energy over a larger area, so each square metre receives less and it is cooler.
